title: The Night of Broken Glass
pull: Glass in the streets by morning

facts.text: On the night of 9 to 10 November 1938, Nazi mobs attacked Jewish people, homes, shops, and synagogues across Germany, Austria, and the Sudetenland.

The pretext was the shooting of a German diplomat, Ernst vom Rath, in Paris on 7 November by Herschel Grynszpan, a 17 year old Polish Jew whose parents had just been deported from Germany. Vom Rath died on 9 November.
Propaganda Minister Joseph Goebbels gave a fiery speech in Munich that evening, and the violence was organized with Hitler's backing.
The U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum counts more than 1,400 synagogues burned or destroyed, and thousands of Jewish owned stores and businesses wrecked.
Hundreds of Jewish people died in the violence and its aftermath.
About 26,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to the Dachau, Buchenwald, and Sachsenhausen concentration camps, where hundreds more died.
The name, Reichskristallnacht, referred to the broken glass that lined the streets. In English it is often called the Night of Broken Glass.
Afterward the regime fined Germany's Jews one billion Reichsmarks and seized the insurance money owed for the damage.
President Franklin D. Roosevelt recalled the U.S. ambassador to Germany, Hugh Wilson, for consultation, and Britain let aid groups organize the Kindertransport to bring Jewish children to safety.

sources.title: Kristallnacht, Holocaust Encyclopedia, United States Holocaust Memorial Museum

photoNote: The burned out synagogue in Frankfurt Hoechst, photographed on 10 November 1938, the morning after the pogrom: blackened windows under the Star of David. Unknown photographer, Stadtarchiv Frankfurt am Main (via Wikimedia Commons), tagged public domain as an anonymous work more than 70 years old; Commons warns the tag does not settle U.S. status. Alternative: the Eisenach synagogue burning, 9 November 1938 (Commons, only 768 px, same anonymous license).
photoCredit: The burned out synagogue in Frankfurt Hoechst, 10 November 1938. Unknown photographer, Stadtarchiv Frankfurt am Main, public domain.

declassified.fact: At his press conference on 15 November 1938, Roosevelt read a short statement: 'I myself could scarcely believe that such things could occur in a twentieth century civilization.' It did not mention Hitler or the German government by name.

sources.title: Franklin D. Roosevelt, The Five Hundredth Press Conference (Excerpts), 15 November 1938, The American Presidency Project

body:
By morning, broken glass lined the streets. More than 1,400 synagogues had been burned or destroyed.

9 November 1938. Through the night, Nazi mobs attacked Jewish people, homes, shops, and synagogues across Germany, Austria, and the Sudetenland. The violence was organized with Hitler's backing, after Joseph Goebbels gave a fiery speech in Munich that evening.

Hundreds of Jewish people died. About 26,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to Dachau, Buchenwald, and Sachsenhausen.

Then the regime fined Germany's Jews one billion Reichsmarks and seized the insurance money owed for the damage.

This is the burned out synagogue in Frankfurt Hoechst the next day.
